titel: Backtests and their sources of error
kurz: Why every methodological error in a backtest distorts the result in the same direction, and which figures make a test reliable.

bloecke.md:
A backtest does not answer whether a rule works. It shows what result the rule would have achieved if it had been applied to a past that was already known when the rule was formulated.

A single quantity is estimated: the expected value per trade. This estimate has a standard error and depends on every decision in the test design, that is, on the data set, the period, the execution assumption and the number of variants tested. The classic errors almost never work in both directions. Look-ahead, survivorship, costs set too low and overfitting all make the result look better than it is. A backtest with a surprisingly good result should therefore first be examined for such errors, and only then can the result count as a finding.

## Splitting the data and walk-forward analysis

In-sample refers to the part of the data in which you may search, discard and readjust. Out-of-sample refers to a section that remains untouched until the very end and is evaluated exactly once. The second definition must be taken strictly. If the rule is changed and retested after a disappointing out-of-sample result, the section then belongs to the in-sample data. This cannot be undone, so untouched data are used up after a single use.

How much you set aside matters less than what the reserved section contains. If it contains only calm upward months, it tests nothing. It must contain at least one regime for which the rule was not built, for example a crash, a turn in the interest rate cycle or a phase of high volatility.

[[Walk-forward analysis]] divides the reserved section into many small ones. You optimise on one window, test on the immediately following, untouched section and then move both windows forward. At the end, only the test sections are strung together. Only this combined curve counts as the result. The optimisation runs look considerably better but are not part of it. This safeguard also has a limit that is often overlooked. Window length, step size and optimisation target were likewise chosen only after the data had been examined. If, in addition, you add a filter after a flat result and repeat the entire run, the test windows have been used up a second time.

bloecke.titel: Sections that count in a walk-forward analysis
bloecke.unter: In each step, optimisation takes place in the left window and testing in the right one; the result curve consists only of windows that were never touched before their evaluation.

bloecke.md:
## Number of variants tested

The more variants are tested, the better the best of them looks, even if not a single one has a real edge. This follows from distribution theory. If you assume N variants with a true Sharpe of zero and independent, normally distributed returns, the best in-sample Sharpe follows the expected value of the maximum of N random draws, divided by the square root of the number of years observed. With five years of daily data, around 50 variants are enough for an expected best Sharpe of 1.0. A value of this level is regarded in presentations as proof of skill.

Bailey, Borwein, López de Prado and Zhu made this calculation well known. It is the basis for the deflated Sharpe ratio, which adjusts for the number of trials and the skewness of returns, and for the probability of backtest overfitting.

bloecke.titel: Best in-sample Sharpe from N trials with pure noise
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation with five years of daily data and N independent variants with a true Sharpe of zero. From around 50 trials, the expected best value is 1.0.

bloecke.md: Without stating how many variants were tested, a backtest metric is the result of a selection and not a measurement. All trials must be counted, that is, every parameter value in the grid, every idea that was discarded after a look at the curve, and also runs by others on the same data set.

There is therefore no fixed value for the number of permitted parameters; it follows from a budget of trials. Each additional free parameter multiplies the number of trials instead of just adding a few. Three parameters with ten tested values each result in a thousand trials. If these trials were independent, the expected best random Sharpe with five years of daily data would already be around 1.45. However, neighbouring parameter values usually produce similar trades, so the variants in a grid are correlated. For a grid, the value is therefore more of an upper limit.

According to a rule of thumb that cannot be derived rigorously, no more than two freely chosen parameters should be optimised with less than ten years of data history. The remaining parameters must also form a plateau. If 18 periods work but 17 and 19 do not, then 18 is a lucky hit and not a usable parameter value. Because of the same multiple testing problem, Harvey, Liu and Zhu call for a t-statistic above 3.0 for new signals instead of the otherwise usual 2.0.

bloecke.text: most claimed research findings in financial economics are likely false
bloecke.quelle: Harvey, Liu and Zhu (2016), Review of Financial Studies

bloecke.md:
## Biases in the data

A look-ahead bias arises in the implementation in code, not in the trading idea. A signal derived from a day's closing price cannot be executed at that closing price. The same group of errors includes balance sheet figures as of the reporting date instead of the publication date, data series corrected later, today's index composition in a test from 2012, and a US closing price used as a signal for an execution in Frankfurt on the same afternoon. As a cross-check, it is enough to shift all signals one bar later. If the edge disappears as a result, it was based on data that were not yet available at the time of trading.

Survivorship bias, by contrast, lies in the data set. A historical test using the current contents of a price database contains no insolvencies, no delistings and no takeovers at depressed prices. Wirecard was a DAX constituent until 2020 and filed for insolvency in June 2020. In many freely accessible price sources, the security no longer exists today. What is needed, therefore, is [[point-in-time data]], which contain constituents and ratios in the state in which they existed on the simulated trading day.

bloecke.md:
## Trading costs and slippage

The costs per [[round turn]] consist of the order fee for entry and exit, half the spread on each side and the [[slippage]]. Most strategies already fail on paper because of these costs. With total costs of 0.10% per round turn on the nominal volume traded, the costs of a strategy that moves the entire capital with each round turn add up to 25 percentage points at 250 round turns a year and to 100 percentage points at 1,000 round turns. Because the costs of each round turn are deducted from the capital remaining at the time, the capital at the end of the year is around 22% or around 63% lower respectively than without these costs. Trading frequency is therefore the most important single lever, more important than any signal.

Slippage is the difference between the price the backtest assumes and the price you get on execution. It must be distinguished from the spread. Slippage arises with market orders in low-volume phases, with execution at the opening after news and above all with stops. A stop-loss guarantees that the order is triggered, but not the price. Across a price gap, execution takes place at the next tradable price. A test that executes every stop exactly at the stop level therefore leaves out the losses that are largest when it really matters.

Using $1.7 trillion of real execution data from 21 developed markets, Frazzini, Israel and Moskowitz showed that institutional trading costs are considerably lower than previously estimated. This applies to patient, algorithmically distributed execution, but not to private investors who enter and exit leveraged products at market prices.

bloecke.titel: From the backtest curve to the net result
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation with 180 round turns a year without leverage and, per round turn, 0.04% fee, 0.04% spread and 0.02% slippage; tax of 26.375% is then due on the remaining profit.

bloecke.md: Costs relate to the volume traded. With leverage, you move a multiple of your own capital. With fivefold leverage, 0.10% per round turn therefore becomes 0.50% of equity, plus financing costs. Leverage does not change the expected value per euro traded. Per euro of equity, it multiplies gain, loss and costs in the same proportion, and with them the expected value. A backtest that relates costs to equity instead of the nominal amount understates them by the leverage factor for every leveraged strategy.

## Required number of trades

Whether a result can be distinguished from zero at all does not depend on the level of the return. What matters is the ratio of the edge to the dispersion and the number of trades. The test statistic is the t-statistic of the average trade return.

bloecke.erklaerung: The t-statistic only grows with the square root of the number of trades. To double the t-statistic, four times the number of trades is therefore needed.
variablen: average result per trade, measured in R (R = the capital risked per trade)
standard deviation of trade results in R
bloecke.beispiel: With E = 0.10 R and s = 1.0 R, t = 0.10 × √n. For t = 2, 400 trades are needed; for the hurdle of t = 3 called for by Harvey, Liu and Zhu, as many as 900.

bloecke.titel: Required number of trades by edge (illustrative calculation, last column showing the duration for t = 3 at 180 trades a year)

bloecke.md: For systems with infrequent signals, this is a problem. A weekly chart system with twelve trades a year reaches 120 trades in ten years. For t = 3, the edge would then have to be around 0.27 of the dispersion. That is possible, but it is a strong claim that can neither be proven nor refuted with these data. If no profit remains after removing the five best trades, the result is based on a few lucky strikes.

A backtest curve shows the result before tax. Capital income is subject to 25% flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) under Section 32d(1) EStG (Income Tax Act), plus 5.5% solidarity surcharge on that under Section 4 SolzG 1995 (Solidarity Surcharge Act), together 26.375%. Three points systematically distort the test. First, the saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) of €1,000 per person (Section 20(9) EStG) is used up after a few weeks with an active strategy. Second, income-related expenses (Werbungskosten) such as data feeds, software and seminars are expressly not deductible under the flat-rate withholding tax (Section 20(9) EStG). They reduce the return but not the tax. Third, losses from share sales may only be offset against gains from share sales (Section 20(6) sentence 4 EStG). A test that nets share losses against gains from derivative transactions (Termingeschäfte) assumes an offsetting that does not exist. The details of the loss pots (Verlusttöpfe) follow later in this module.

## Psychological sources of error

The methodological errors make up the smaller part of the problems; the larger part lies with the tester. Hindsight bias (Fischhoff, 1975) makes every turning point look obvious on the historical chart. In a clean test, the right-hand part of the chart is therefore covered and the test is recorded bar by bar. Confirmation bias (Wason, 1960) leads you to test variants that could support the thesis instead of those that would refute it. The illusion of control also has measurable consequences. Fenton-O'Creevy and colleagues found that traders with a high illusion of control had significantly poorer scores in analysis and risk management and made a lower contribution to profits.

bloecke.titel: Define the test protocol in advance
bloecke.md: Before the first run, the following are set down in writing: universe, period, reserved section, cost assumption per round turn, parameter grid with the maximum permitted number of variants, and stopping criterion. After that, the protocol applies. Any later deviation is added with a date and a reason and counts as an additional trial. The procedure comes from empirical research. It is the only effective protection against your memory of the original specifications shifting after the fact.

## What a passed test tells you

A passed test does not show that the rule works. It shows that it has not yet been refuted under the documented assumptions. The real out-of-sample test only begins with real money. Execution quality, taxes and your own behaviour come into play, and the data set is at its shortest here. That is why the stopping rule belongs in the protocol. It specifies at what drawdown and after how many trades without the expected edge the strategy is discontinued. A stopping rule that is only set during a loss no longer serves its purpose.

mitnehmen: All the classic backtest errors make the result look better, so a surprisingly good test should first be checked for errors.
The number of variants tested is part of the result, because with five years of daily data, around 50 independent trials produce a best Sharpe of 1.0 from noise alone.
Out-of-sample data can only be used once, because any readjustment after looking at the results turns the test into a further optimisation.
Trading frequency is the strongest lever, because at 0.10% per round turn and 250 round turns a year, costs add up to 25 percentage points and reduce the final capital by around 22%.
With fewer than a few hundred trades, an edge cannot be statistically distinguished from zero.

begriffe.text: Rolling test procedure in which optimisation takes place on one data window and testing on the immediately following, untouched section. Both windows are then moved forward. Only the test sections strung together count as the result.
Difference between the price a backtest assumes for execution and the price actually achieved. Slippage arises with market orders, with thin liquidity and with price gaps across a stop level.

A complete trading transaction consisting of entry and exit. The round-turn costs, made up of order fee, spread and slippage, are expressed relative to the nominal volume traded and multiplied by the trading frequency.

Data set that contains prices, ratios and index compositions in the state in which they were available on each historical day, including securities that later became insolvent or were delisted. Such data are a prerequisite for tests free of look-ahead and survivorship bias.

Adjustment to the Sharpe ratio proposed by Bailey and López de Prado that takes into account the number of strategy variants tested, the length of the time series, and the skewness and kurtosis of returns.
